Compare subsequence patterns between groups

Source: R/sequence_compare.R
sequence_compare.Rd

sequence_compare() compares how often short subsequences occur in two or more groups of sequences. For each pattern length in sub it counts every k-gram (a run of k consecutive states, such as "A->B->C") in each group, keeps the patterns that are frequent enough in every group, and returns a net_sequence_comparison whose pattern table has one row per pattern with its count, proportion and standardised residual in each group and, optionally, a permutation or chi-square test of whether its frequency differs between the groups. It takes a grouped network, a single network or wide sequences with a grouping.

A residual says how far a group's count of a pattern lies from the count expected if pattern and group were independent, in approximately standard-normal units (Haberman, 1973); a positive value means the pattern is more frequent in that group than independence predicts. The p-values are adjusted across every pattern tested. The permutation test treats the sequence as the unit, while the chi-square test treats every occurrence as independent, which overstates the evidence when occurrences within a sequence depend on each other (see Details). Patterns of different lengths overlap (each 3-gram contains two 2-grams), so their tests are not independent of each other. sequence_patterns() with group asks the related question of whether a pattern is present in more sequences of one group.

Usage

sequence_compare(
  x,
  group = NULL,
  sub = 3:5,
  min_freq = 5L,
  test = c("permutation", "chisq", "none"),
  iter = 1000L,
  adjust = "fdr",
  actor = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'net_sequence_comparison'
print(x, n = 10L, digits = 2L, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_sequence_comparison'
summary(object, format = c("wide", "long"), ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_sequence_comparison'
plot(
  x,
  top_n = 10L,
  style = c("auto", "pyramid", "heatmap"),
  sort = c("statistic", "frequency"),
  alpha = 0.05,
  show_residuals = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

The sequences:

  • a netobject_group, from build_network() with group or from a clustering, whose groups are compared;

  • a netobject, tna model or cograph_network built from sequences;

  • a wide data frame with numbered position columns, as in build_network(), or a character matrix, one row per sequence;

  • a group_tna, read as the group of networks it converts to (see as_netobject()).

Every input except a netobject_group needs group. One-hot data, association networks and data frames with extra columns raise nestimate_bad_input. With actor, a tna model must keep its metadata, as one built with tna::prepare_data() does. For print() and plot(): a sequence_compare() result.

group

The group of each sequence: the name of a column of a data frame or matrix x (that column is then not read as a position), or a vector with one label per sequence. Ignored for a netobject_group; required otherwise. At least two groups are needed. Sequences with a missing group are left out of the counts with a warning of class nestimate_missing_group. Default NULL.

sub

The pattern lengths to count, positive whole numbers. Lengths longer than the sequences are dropped, and an error is raised when none remains. Default 3:5.

min_freq

The smallest count a pattern must reach in every group to be kept, a positive whole number; when no pattern of any length reaches it, an error is raised. Default 5.

test

The inference: "permutation" (default), "chisq" or "none"; see Details.

iter

The number of permutations for test = "permutation", a positive whole number; ignored otherwise. With iter = 1 the effect size is undefined, and a warning says so. Default 1000.

adjust

The p-value adjustment, any method of stats::p.adjust() ("holm", "hochberg", "hommel", "bonferroni", "BH", "BY", "fdr" or "none"). Default "fdr" (Benjamini-Hochberg).

actor

The column identifying the actor each sequence belongs to, or several columns for nested levels, outermost first (c("Group", "Student")); see Nested data and actor. With several levels, labels are shuffled at the level where they are assigned, within the units above it, and n_actors counts the innermost level. For a netobject_group, netobject or tna model the columns are looked up in the network's $metadata (for example the Group column kept by build_network() when students are nested in teams); for a data frame or matrix x, they are columns of x, which are then not read as positions. Only used with test = "permutation"; with "chisq" or "none" it is ignored with a warning of class nestimate_ignored_argument. Duplicated, missing or empty names, and levels that are not nested outermost first (a level that adds no units below the one before it), raise an error of class nestimate_bad_actor; a column that is absent or has missing values, nestimate_actor_missing; a column that does not give one id per sequence, nestimate_actor_misaligned. Default NULL: every sequence is shuffled on its own.

n

For print(): the number of patterns shown, the first ones of the pattern table. Default 10.

digits

For print(): the decimals of the counts' shares, residuals and effect sizes. Default 2; p-values show 3 significant digits.

...

Not used.

object

For the summary() method: a net_sequence_comparison.

format

For summary(): "wide" (default), the pattern table, one row per pattern with a freq_, prop_ and resid_ column per group; "long", one row per pattern and group, with columns pattern, length, group, count, proportion, residual and the pattern's effect_size (or statistic) and p_value.

top_n

For plot(): the number of patterns drawn, the first ones after ranking by sort. Default 10.

style

For plot(): "auto" (default) draws the back-to-back pyramid for exactly 2 groups and the heatmap for any other number; "pyramid" and "heatmap" force one. "pyramid" with other than 2 groups raises an error.

sort

For plot(): how to pick and order the patterns. "statistic" (default) ranks them by the absolute effect size after a permutation test, by the chi-square statistic after a chi-square test, and by the largest absolute residual without a test. "frequency" ranks them by their total count across the groups.

alpha

For the pyramid: the significance level for the p-value labels. Patterns with p_value < alpha are starred and drawn in bold dark text, the rest in plain grey. Default 0.05. The heatmap and a comparison without a test ignore it.

show_residuals

For the pyramid: whether to print each bar's standardised residual inside it. Default FALSE. The heatmap always prints the residuals.

Value

A net_sequence_comparison object. print() shows the numbers of patterns and groups, the settings and the first n patterns, one row per pattern and group, rounded, and returns its input invisibly; summary() returns the pattern table, a data frame with one row per pattern (format = "long": one row per pattern and group); plot() draws the residuals of the top patterns (see Plot styles). The object holds:

patterns

The pattern table, one row per k-gram kept. Always: pattern, length, and per group freq_<group> (the count), prop_<group> (the count as a share of all k-grams of that length in the group, rare ones included) and resid_<group> (the standardised residual). With test = "permutation" also effect_size and p_value; with test = "chisq", statistic and p_value. The p-values are adjusted. Rows are ordered by ascending p_value (ties by the larger absolute effect size, or the larger statistic) when a test was run, and by descending largest absolute residual otherwise.

groups

The group names, sorted.

n_patterns

The number of rows of the pattern table: the patterns that reach min_freq in every group.

params

The settings used: sub (after dropping lengths longer than the sequences), min_freq, test, iter and adjust; with actor and test = "permutation" also actor (the column name), n_actors (the number of distinct actors among the sequences with a group) and design ("between" when every actor lies in one group, "within" when every actor lies in several, "mixed" otherwise). With several actor levels, n_actors counts the innermost level, design reads "<level>: <design> (<n> actors)" for every level, and actor_levels is a data frame with one row per level: level, n_actors, n_pure and n_crossed (the units the shuffle met at that level, inside crossed units above, in one group or in several) and design ("not opened" when no unit above was crossed).

Details

The standardised residuals come from the 2 x G table of the pattern's counts against the counts of all other k-grams of the same length in each group, with the formula (o - e) / sqrt(e * (1 - r/N) * (1 - c/N)). They are always computed, whatever test is. A k-gram that spans a missing position is not counted.

test chooses the inference:

"permutation"

Shuffles the group labels across sequences iter times and recomputes, for each pattern, the Euclidean norm of its row of differences between observed and expected counts in the patterns-by-groups table of every pattern observed at that length (expected under independence), whether or not min_freq keeps it, so the filter does not change the null distribution of a reported pattern. It asks whether the pattern's distribution is associated with group membership at the level of the sequence, which respects the sequence as the unit of analysis but has little power when there are few sequences. The p-value is (b + 1) / (iter + 1), where b counts the permutations with a statistic at least as large as the observed one, so it cannot fall below 1 / (iter + 1). The effect size is the observed statistic minus the mean of the permuted ones, divided by their standard deviation (taken as 1 when the permuted statistics do not vary; with iter = 1 the effect size is NA, since at least two permutations are needed). The shuffles use R's random number generator: call base::set.seed() first for reproducible p-values.

"chisq"

Runs stats::chisq.test() on each pattern's 2 x G table (with Yates' continuity correction when there are two groups). It asks whether the groups' streams of k-grams produce the pattern at different rates, treating every occurrence as an independent event: it is fast and has power with few sequences, but the independence it assumes is optimistic when sequences are strongly autocorrelated.

"none"

No test; the counts, proportions and residuals only.

The p-values are adjusted once across all patterns of all lengths, with stats::p.adjust().

Nested data and actor

The permutation test treats every sequence as exchangeable. When several sequences come from the same actor (sessions of one student, students of one team), they resemble each other, and shuffling single sequences understates how much the pattern counts vary by chance: when the groups are made of different actors, the test then rejects too often. actor names the column identifying the actor of each sequence, and the shuffle respects it, as in permutation() (Good, 2005; Anderson & ter Braak, 2003): an actor whose sequences all lie in one group keeps them together and moves as a whole, its group label shuffled among the other such actors; an actor with sequences in several groups (a within-actor design, such as pre and post sessions of each student) has its labels shuffled among its own sequences only, so it keeps its number of sequences in each group. Mixed designs combine the two. Use it whenever the groups are made of different actors; for groups within actors it costs little. The observed counts, proportions and residuals do not change; only the p-values and effect sizes do. Sequences with a missing group keep it. With few actors there are few distinct ways to shuffle them, and a warning of class nestimate_few_actors is raised when no p-value could fall below 0.05.

Several columns, outermost first (actor = c("Group", "Student")), are nested levels, the unit at each level being the combination of its column with the ones before it. The labels are then shuffled at the level where they are assigned, within the units above it, as in permutation(): units whose sequences all lie in one group exchange their labels with the other such units of the same parent (all top-level units at the first level), each moving whole; a unit with sequences in several groups is opened at the next level, and inside such a unit of the last level single sequences exchange labels. One column runs exactly the one-level scheme above.

Plot styles

plot() draws the standardised residuals of the top top_n patterns, prints the plot and returns the ggplot invisibly (NULL, with a message, when there are no patterns). style = "auto" (the default) picks the style from the number of groups:

"pyramid"

Back-to-back bars of each pattern's proportion in the two groups, each bar shaded by that group's standardised residual (the colour saturates at plus or minus 3), with the (adjusted) p-value in the gap between the bars when a test was run. Needs exactly 2 groups.

"heatmap"

One tile per pattern and group, coloured by the standardised residual (the colour saturates at plus or minus 3) and labelled with its value. Works for any number of groups.

The residuals are filled whatever test was chosen, so both styles work after test = "none".

References

Anderson, M. J., & ter Braak, C. J. F. (2003). Permutation tests for multi-factorial analysis of variance. Journal of Statistical Computation and Simulation, 73(2), 85-113. (the actor shuffle)

Good, P. (2005). Permutation, Parametric, and Bootstrap Tests of Hypotheses (3rd ed.). Springer. (the actor shuffle)

Haberman, S. J. (1973). The analysis of residuals in cross-classified tables. Biometrics, 29(1), 205–220. (standardised residuals)

Benjamini, Y. & Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B, 57(1), 289–300. (the default adjust = "fdr")

Examples

set.seed(1)
seqs <- data.frame(
  V1 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 60, TRUE),
  V2 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 60, TRUE),
  V3 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 60, TRUE),
  V4 = sample(LETTERS[1:4], 60, TRUE)
)
grp <- rep(c("X", "Y"), 30)
net <- build_network(seqs, method = "relative")
res <- sequence_compare(net, group = grp, sub = 2:3, test = "chisq")
# \donttest{
# Students are nested in teams, and Achiever is a team-level label:
# shuffle whole teams, not single students
net <- build_network(group_regulation_long, method = "relative",
                     actor = "Actor", action = "Action", time = "Time",
                     group = "Achiever")
set.seed(1)
sequence_compare(net, sub = 2, iter = 100, actor = "Group")
